Eat.

fields.explain:
Mild emphasis/pressure: used when an action is needed right away, especially in safety situations.
Can be softened with よ/ね:片付け なさいね。/早く寝 なさいよ。
Instructional texts: ～しなさい was often replaced by ～しなさいこと in older books; nowadays ～こと/～こと is commonly used。
Combined with an indirect prohibitive adverb: もうそれ以上言わ ないで、早く謝り なさい。

• A directive command or reminder addressed to subordinates or people close to you (children, students, subordinates).
• The nuance is stronger than ～てください (asking/request), but softer than 命令形（～しろ／～しなさい＜～しろ）.
• Often used in education, in announcing rules, or when emphasizing something that "should be done right away".
• Not used with superiors/customers; use ～てください／ご～ください instead。
fields.notes:
• Colloquial contracted form: しな／やりな（with a casual nuance).
• "～なさいませ" appears in old-fashioned retail service language: ご利用なさいませ（very polite, old style).
• Combining with prohibition: ～てはいけません／～ないでください to prohibit, and ～なさい to indicate what should be done.
mistakes: Wrong form: × 書くなさい → ○ 書きなさい（drop ます).
Using it with superiors is rude; choose ～てください／ご覧ください…
Confusion with prohibition: "～な" is a prohibition, not ～なさい.
Pronunciation of 来なさい: きなさい, not こなさい.
Overuse makes the sentence sound harsh; avoid it in customer service.

fields.explain:
Polite: ～なくても いいです ／～なくても かまいません .
Gentle; reassures or relaxes a requirement.
With A/N: expresses a minimum standard that does not need to be met.
To emphasize "should not": use ～ないほうがいい instead of ～なくてもいい.

• Gives permission not to do an action or have a quality / does not require it: "you don't have to ...".
• Reduces the burden and presents an option; it does not completely negate doing the action.
• Practical opposite of ～なくてはいけない／～なければならない.
• Often used in instructions, soft rules, and customer service.
fields.notes:
• Past form/hypothetical: 来なくてもよかった（didn't need to come). Easily confused with the regret expression ～ばよかった.
• Polite double negative: ～なくてもよろしい（very polite, used in written notices).
• Emphasizing the option: ～ても～なくてもいい（Either doing it or not doing it is fine）.
mistakes: Forgetting "で" with N/na: ×会員なくてもいい → 〇会員でなくてもいい.
Confusion with "should not": ×行かなくてもいい（when you mean "you shouldn't go"）→ 〇行かないほうがいい.
Wrong level of politeness: with customers use ～なくてもかまいません instead of ～なくてもいいよ.
In exams, a double-negative trap: "必ずしも～なくてもいい" = "you don't necessarily have to ...".

fields.explain: ◎ A sentence pattern that compares two things to show which one is superior or inferior.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: Used to compare two things or matters, where one (noun ②) exceeds the other (noun ①) in degree: (noun ②) > (noun ①). Usually not used in negative sentences.
examples: 1. ①私より弟のほうが背が高いです。
My younger brother is taller than me.
2. ②前のテキストのほうがこのテキストよりよかったです。
The previous textbook was better than this textbook.
3. ③私はご飯よりパンのほうをよく食べます。
I eat bread more often than rice.

examples: After class, I'll ask the teacher a question.
After eating lunch, I took a walk.
Would you like to go for a drink after work?
There is a meeting after this.
After the rain, the air becomes clean.

fields.explain:
In spoken language "あとで" is common; in written language "あとに/後に" can be used.
"で" emphasizes the setting in time in which B happens "after A"; "に" emphasizes the point in time.
Do not use ～のあとで with a specific clock time: use 3時以降／3時のちに（formal）/3時過ぎに instead.
Natural order: A finishes safely and then B happens; suited to actions that need preparation beforehand.

Expresses that action B happens after A has been completed: A の/た あとで、B。
There may or may not be a time gap between A and B; it does not have to be "right after".
Difference from ～てから: ～てから often suggests "right after / do it and then immediately".
With numerical time expressions (3時,三日,三時間): use ～後（ご）/ ～以降 instead of ～のあとで.
fields.notes:
"あとで" on its own = "later / in a while": あとで電話します。
"直後（ちょくご）" = "right after":試合の直後にインタビューがあった。
"のちに" (後に・のちに) formal/literary:彼はのちに大統領となる。
mistakes: Wrong tense: ×食べるあとで → ✓食べたあとで.
Using it with a clock time: ×3時のあとで会いましょう → ✓3時以降に会いましょう.
Confusion with ～てから: when "right after" is required, choose ～てから, not ～たあとで.
A noun that is not an event: ×机のあとで掃除する → ✓掃除のあとで休む／机を片付けてから休む.

examples: I wonder if it will rain tomorrow.
I wonder if these clothes will suit him.
I wonder if we'll make it in time.
I wonder what I should do.
I wonder if it's really all right.
fields.explain:
Feminine, gentle nuance; men usually use かな/かなあ.
Used in casual, everyday conversation; in work or formal exchanges use でしょうか/かどうか.
Add ね to soften it: ～かしらね; add のかしら for a nuance of explaining/emphasizing the reason behind the conjecture.

• A sentence-final particle meaning "I wonder…"; often used by women; similar to かな (neutral/used more by men).
• Expresses gentle reflection without requiring a direct answer; used when talking to yourself or when asking for someone's opinion in an indirect way.
• The intonation usually rises at the end of the sentence when it is a real question: ～かしら↑
• In polite speech, use ～でしょうか（ね） instead of ～ですかしら to avoid sounding stylistically off.
fields.notes:
• In polite letters, replace it with でしょうか／お伺いできますでしょうか to suit the style.
• Polite expressions like "～してもよろしいかしら" exist in the speech of middle-aged and older women.
• Archaic form: ～かしらん (literary, playful/old-fashioned).
mistakes: × 本当ですかしら → ○ 本当かしら／本当でしょうか.
Using it with superiors/customers: avoid ～かしら and choose でしょうか.
Men who use it too much sound stylistically off; use かな instead.

fields.meaning: A casual way of expressing that you are wondering to yourself. ③ expresses hesitation about what to do.; I hope… (in the form ～ないかな(あ))
fields.connection: V/A plain form + かな(あ) / N/Na + かな(あ)
examples: I wonder if I can get in.
I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.
Maybe I'll go. What should I do?
I wish something interesting would happen.
Tomorrow's party... should I go, or skip it? What should I do?
"This problem is a bit hard, but I wonder if I can do it." "You can, I'm sure."
fields.explain:
Used at the end of a sentence with a light, rising-and-falling tone; usually when talking to yourself or to people close to you.
Not used to question someone directly; for a polite question use ～でしょうか／ますか.
Traditionally women used かしら; nowadays かなあ is used by both men and women, and かな (without あ) is more neutral.
かなあ is usually preceded by the plain form; です／ます + かなあ exists but is slightly formal and not very natural in written language.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: I wonder…, probably…
examples: 1. 明日、晴れるかなあ。
I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.
2. 彼、来てくれるかなあ。
I wonder if he'll come.
3. 日本語、もっと上手に話せるかなあ。
I wonder if I'll be able to speak Japanese better.
4. この問題、間に合うかなあ。
I wonder if I'll finish this problem in time.
5. 値段、もう少し安くならないかなあ。
I wish the price would come down a little more.
6. 大丈夫かなあ…。
I wonder if it's all right… meaning_vi: Won't it…?, I hope…, will it… or not? ⏐ explain: Used to express your own hope, or your own doubt about some matter
It mostly implies worry or unease about what is happening ⏐ examples: 1. バス、早く来ないかなあ。
I wish the bus would come soon.
2. この実験、うまくいくかな。
I wonder if this experiment will go well.
3. 今日、富士山が見えるかなあ。
I wonder if we'll be able to see Mt. Fuji today.
mistakes: Using かなあ to ask a stranger directly → not polite enough. Use ～でしょうか／ますか instead.
Wrong polite form: ×静かだかなあ → 〇静かかなあ (colloquial).
Confusion with a question using か: かなあ needs no "?" and does not require an answer.
JLPT: distinguish かなあ (spoken language) from だろうか (written language) and かしら (feminine nuance).

examples: It might rain this evening.
What he's saying might be right.
We practiced hard, so we've gotten stronger. We might be able to win tomorrow's match.
"Are you free next week?"
"Ali still hasn't come, has he? He's late."
I have a headache. It might be because I didn't sleep much last night.
fields.explain:
A reserved nuance that avoids asserting; suitable when you want to be polite/not impose.
In reports/academic writing, it can be replaced with 可能性がある (formal).
Degree of certainty: に違いない ＞ だろう／でしょう ＞ かもしれない.

• Expresses a judgment about possibility, with lower certainty than だろう／でしょう.
• Often combined with adverbs: もしかすると／もしかしたら／ひょっとすると to emphasize "who knows".
• The past is used to make a conjecture about something that already happened: 行ったかもしれない／学生だったかもしれない.
fields.notes:
• Spelling: かも知れない (kanji) is also correct; it is usually written かもしれない (hiragana).
• Not used directly before a command/order; if needed, change it to a mild recommendation.
• Adding たぶん tends to be redundant; it is more natural with もしかしたら/ひょっとすると.
mistakes: × 学生ですかもしれない → ○ 学生かもしれない.
な形容詞 in the present does not take だ: × 静かだかもしれない → ○ 静かかもしれない.
Forgetting "だった" in the past: × 学生だかもしれなかった → ○ 学生だったかもしれない.

fields.explain: ◎ 「ある」expresses possession, like「持っている」. Besides concrete objects, it can be used with abstract things or things with a psychological meaning.

examples: Please let me explain once more.
Please let me rest for a bit.
Please let me go home first.
Please let me take a photo.

Would you allow me to speak on this matter?
fields.explain:
Formal: ～させていただけますか／～させていただきたいです。
Casual: ～させて（もらって）／～させてね（within your own group).
In business: as a humble announcement, "ご連絡 させていただきます "。
Avoid using it with来る: "来させてください" sounds awkward; people usually say "伺わせてください／行かせてください".

• Asks the listener for permission for the speaker to do an action: "let me …/please allow me to …".
• Emphasizes the speaker's volition/intention more than ～てもいいですか (which only asks whether it is allowed).
• The nuance can be somewhat strong/imposing; in formal contexts use ～させていただけますか to soften it.
• Used for actions the speaker does themselves; not used to "ask someone else to do something".
fields.notes:
• "～させていただく" should be used when: there is permission, it benefits the listener, or the speaker is grateful; avoid overusing it for no reason.
• Combines with keigo nouns: ご挨拶／ご連絡／ご報告＋させていただく.
• Negative causative asking permission: ～させないでください（please don't make/let me do it; please let me not do it） is rare; consider the context carefully.
meaning_vi: asking for permission.
examples: 1. 「疲れたので、少し休ませてください」
「I'm tired, so please let me rest for a bit.」
2. 「そのゲーム、おもしろそうね。わたしにもやらせて」
「That game looks fun. Let me play too.」
3. 「いつもごちそうになっているので、たまにはわたしに払わせてください」
「You always treat me, so please let me pay once in a while.」
meaning_vi: Could you let me ~?
explain: Used to ask the other person for permission to do something yourself.
They all mean the same thing, but the level of politeness differs. Specifically:
Vさせて　ください　＜　Vさせて　もらえます　＜　Vさせて　もらえませんか。
See also: review how to conjugate verbs in the causative form (使役形）：See
examples: 1. ちょっと気分が悪いので、早く帰らせてください。
I'm not feeling very well, so please let me go home early.
2. あなたの会社のお話を聞かせてください。
Please tell me about your company.
3. 手を洗わせてください。
Please let me wash my hands.
mistakes: Using it to ask someone else to do something: ×説明させてください＝please explain to me → wrong meaning; this pattern means "let me explain".
Wrong causative: ×見らせてください → ✓見させてください；×行きさせて → ✓行かせてください。
Too direct with superiors/customers: switch to ～させていただけますか.
The JLPT often asks you to distinguish it from ～てもいいですか (neutral permission) and ～てください (request).

fields.connection: V causative form + られる / くる + こさせられる / やる + やらせられる
examples: When I was a child, I was forced to eat vegetables I didn't like.
My boss asked me to come in on my day off, and I ended up being made to work.
This movie makes you think about social issues.
Because of the accident, we were made to take a detour and arrived late.
His stories about his failures always make me laugh.
fields.explain:
Passive + forced nuance: usually comes with feelings of displeasure, annoyance, or reluctance.
In written/argumentative language, 〜させられる can be used abstractly (状況に〜させられる), weakening the nuance of "someone forces you" and emphasizing "the circumstances make you".
The contracted form -される of五段 verbs is natural in conversation:行かされる,書かされる,待たされる (from待たせられる).

• 〜させられる: "be made/forced to do…"; the subject feels reluctant/unwilling.
• Common formula: Nは/が Nに Vさせられる (be made to do V by N).
• With 五段 verbs: the contracted form 〜される (行かされる, 書かされる, 読まされる) is very common in spoken language; the full form 〜せられる is more formal.
• Some fixed expressions mean "make you think/feel": 考えさせられる, 感心させられる, 驚かされる (from 驚く).
fields.notes:
• 待たされる is the established form in practice (considered more natural than 待たせられる).
• Emotion verbs often use the form 〜させられる/〜される to say "made to feel": 考えさせられる, 驚かされる, 感動させられる.
• Avoid repeating a long subject: compared with Aさんに私は行かされるより, "私はAさんに…" is more concise.
meaning_vi: Be made to do something => Can't help (feeling)~
explain: ◎ The「られる」 part of the passive is attached after the「させる」 of the causative pattern. 「びっくりさせられる」(be made to jump in surprise) expresses the same event as 「びっくりする」(be surprised), but adding「～させられる」adds a feeling of unexpected, involuntary surprise.
examples: 1. 青木さんのまじめなことには、みんな感心させられている。
Everyone can't help admiring how hardworking Mr. Aoki is.
2. 山の上から見た景色の美しさには、感動させられました。
I couldn't help being moved by the beauty of the view from the top of the mountain.
mistakes: Confusing 五段 forms: 書く → 書かされる (colloquial) / 書かせられる (formal). Avoid "書きさせられる" (incorrect).
Missing the agent marker に: "上司に残業させられた" (correct); dropping に can make it ambiguous.
Confusing the meaning with 〜なければならない: "行かなければならない" is obligation, without the nuance of "being forced by someone" that "行かされる" has.
The JLPT often asks about the easily confused pair 考えさせられる vs 考えられる (ability/inference). Distinguish them by context.
